Telling infrastructure stories well
body:
Jointly launched by the Development Bureau and the Construction Industry Council, the “Hong Kong Infrastructure NO. 1” campaign seeks to deepen public understanding of the city’s infrastructure projects.

 

Through guided tours, interactive workshops, exhibitions and tailored teaching materials, the campaign shares professional engineering knowledge in an engaging and accessible way, allowing young people to explore careers in the construction industry.

 

Awe-inspiring visit

A group of primary school pupils toured the education centre at Plant Number 3 of the Kai Tak District Cooling System, where they learnt about the climate challenges facing Hong Kong and how the cooling system works.

 

Interactive exhibits helped the pupils understand the technology behind the system, while a tour of the plant’s core facilities gave them a close-up view of its large-scale machinery and extensive network of pipes.

 

The facility completely defied the expectations of Primary 5 pupil Horace Tang.

 

“I was amazed by the sheer size of the plant and its enormous pipes,” he said.

 

“I think the district cooling system is remarkable because it helps reduce carbon emissions and save energy. The tour has inspired me to become an engineer in the future.”

 

Hands-on learning

The initiative focuses on three key areas: education, public engagement and media promotion.

 

On the education front, the campaign organises guided tours and engineering visits, while also providing a dedicated resource centre, interactive workshops and tailored learning and teaching materials.

 

The construction-themed materials integrate science, technology, engineering, the arts and mathematics, allowing students to explore subjects such as urban planning in an engaging and practical manner.

 

Moving beyond classroom concepts, students actively design their own communities within strict special limits and specific guidelines.

 

Secondary 3 pupil Chui Ki-hin said the workshop transformed his understanding of urban planning.

 

“I used to think urban planning was simple - that you could just arrange buildings like building blocks and connect the necessary utilities,” he said.

 

“However, after taking part in the workshop, I realised that it is much more complicated and that there are many constraints to consider.”

 

Even producing a small model required considerable thought and effort.

 

“It took me about 45 minutes just to complete this small model. I can only imagine how much more challenging it is to plan a real city.”

 

International recognition

Apart from its education initiatives, the campaign reaches the community through videos, social media content, exhibitions, quizzes and other public engagement activities.

 

The campaign’s impact has resonated far beyond Hong Kong. At the 23rd International Business Awards, the promotional initiative triumphed across 10 different categories - capturing six Gold and three Silver awards, as well as one Bronze.

 

“The aim is to use interesting and heartfelt stories to help the public more easily understand the advanced technologies adopted in infrastructure projects that we see in everyday life, and appreciate the craftsmanship spirit of our construction industry professionals,” Principal Assistant Secretary for Development (Works) Chris Ng said.

 

He added that Hong Kong’s global standing in engineering would not be possible without the commitment and expertise of industry professionals.

 

Construction Industry Council General Manager - Corporate Communications Hanks Lee said the trickiest part of the campaign was figuring out how to share professional engineering know-how in a down-to-earth and lively way.

 

“With the wholehearted support of the industry providing invaluable experience, practical examples and on-site assistance, we were able to tell the story of Hong Kong’s infrastructure.”

 

Looking ahead, the Development Bureau will continue to leverage digital and innovative media to showcase the technological advancement and professionalism of the construction industry. Through these efforts, it aims to deepen public understanding of the vital role infrastructure plays in Hong Kong’s economic, social and livelihood development, while attracting more young people to join the industry and carry forward the spirit of striving for excellence.

Commerce chief joins APEC e-meet
body:
Secretary for Commerce & Economic Development Algernon Yau attended the video conference of the 37th Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) ministerial meeting yesterday evening.

 

The theme for APEC this year is “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together”.

 

During a discussion session, Mr Yau emphasised that member economies must collaborate together through enhanced dialogue and co-operation to achieve shared prosperity amid rapidly evolving global landscape and technological advancements.

 

Citing digital transformation as an example, Mr Yau said that practical co-operation is essential for member economies to harness their respective strengths in digital technologies in a people-centred and inclusive manner. He added that Hong Kong is strengthening its research capacity in frontier technologies and launching programmes to promote public awareness and the responsible use of AI.

 

He urged member economies to continue to strengthen connectivity across various areas to enable the efficient flow of goods, services, capital and people, while narrowing development gaps and creating opportunities region-wide. He added that collaborative efforts among member economies should continue to be guided by the Putrajaya Vision 2040 and the Aotearoa Plan of Action.

 

At another discussion session, Mr Yau noted that enhancing economic integration remains a core objective of APEC, with advancing the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP) as a direction.

 

“As part of Hong Kong's wider efforts to contribute to the FTAAP agenda, we have been actively seeking early accession to the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership. We welcome the establishment of the Accession Working Group for Hong Kong in September this year, and hope that our accession could inject fresh impetus into advancing the FTAAP agenda,” he said.

 

Mr Yau also highlighted the importance of enhancing co-operation to deal with the seismic changes in the trade landscape. As technological advancement increasingly transforms international trade, deepening co-operation in this area is vital for promoting cross-boundary trade and investment. He stated that Hong Kong fully supports the proposed Trade Digitalization Cooperation Framework as a guiding document for future co-operation.

 

He stressed that the multilateral trading system must remain the foundation of regional integration and international trade.

 

“We call on member economies to continue supporting the World Trade Organization (WTO)'s reform agenda, incorporating plurilateral initiatives into the WTO framework, finding a permanent solution for the moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions, and facilitating the Work Programme on Electronic Commerce,” he said.

title: LawTech funding scheme launched
body:
The Department of Justice (DoJ) today officially launched the Funding Scheme for LawTech Solution Subscription by the Hong Kong Legal Sector, aiming to boost the local legal sector’s technological capability and fortify the city’s status as an international legal and dispute resolution hub.

 

The scheme is a policy initiative under the Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address. It will be jointly managed by the Hong Kong Bar Association and the Law Society of Hong Kong, which will handle applications and disburse funds.  

 

Applications are open from today until January 29, 2027. Eligible applicants include sole practitioners, Hong Kong law firms with no more than five partners, and barristers with no more than seven years of call.

 

Deputy Secretary for Justice and Chairman of the Consultation Group on LawTech Development Cheung Kwok-kwan stated that promoting LawTech is a core DoJ policy initiative. He noted that since last year, the DoJ has hosted five rounds of the LexGoTech Roundtables to gather feedback from practitioners, academics and stakeholders.

 

He added that the DoJ is aware that small and medium-sized law firms, as well as junior barristers, are particularly concerned about the financial burden of adopting LawTech tools. The scheme is launched to directly respond to the industry’s needs.

 

He pointed out that small and medium-sized law firms account for about 88% of all law firms in Hong Kong, while junior barristers with less than seven years of call make up about one-third of the total practicing bar. The scheme will lower the barrier to entry and enhance the overall competitiveness of Hong Kong's legal sector.

 

Operating on an actual-expense reimbursement basis, the scheme provides up to $20,000 per applicant for a one-year subscription. Applicants can choose from a designated list of 14 local, Mainland and overseas providers covering legal research, document drafting, workflow management and hearing support.

 

To ensure effectiveness, these service providers will offer transparent pricing alongside technical support and training. The application process consists of four steps.

 

First, applicants must select a provider from the designated list and obtain a written price quotation. Second, they will submit their application to either the Hong Kong Bar Association or the Law Society of Hong Kong.

 

Third, the relevant body will issue a written result, after which successful applicants can subscribe to their chosen service. Finally, applicants submit proof of subscription and payment to their respective professional body to claim reimbursement.

title: FinTech Week opens
body:
The 11th edition of the five-day Hong Kong FinTech Week kicked off today at the Convention & Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai, drawing over 1,000 government and business leaders and around 800 exhibitors and startups.

 

Opening the event, Chief Executive John Lee highlighted the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government’s inaugural Five-Year Plan, underscoring the city’s role as a multi-hub powerhouse and driving regional synergy with Shenzhen and the wider Greater Bay Area through the Northern Metropolis serving as a new “South-North dual engine”.

 

Mr Lee said: “Less than two months ago, the Hong Kong SAR Government unveiled Hong Kong’s first-ever Five-Year Plan for Economic & Social Development. It is closely aligned with the National 15th Five-Year Plan, which sets out a clear direction for Hong Kong to leverage its strengths and better integrate into, and serve, the overall national development.”

 

“Our inaugural Five-Year Plan portrays Hong Kong’s outlook for businesses, investors and innovators, helping you capitalise on the far-reaching promise of Hong Kong – the abundance of opportunities arising from national and global development,” Mr Lee added.

 

Mainland enterprises turned out in force. The Shenzhen Fintech Association brought a delegation for the fourth consecutive year, expanding its group to 20 companies, viewing Hong Kong as an ideal “super-connector” and a strategic springboard for global expansion.

 

Meanwhile, the Zhongguancun Fintech Industry Development Alliance highlighted Hong Kong’s capital market as a vital gateway for scaling Mainland tech firms onto the global stage.

 

The alliance’s Secretary-General added that the city leverages its rich concentration of financial institutions and international talent pool.

 

International delegations also seized the spotlight. A Malaysian delegation focused on artificial intelligence and virtual asset technologies, highlighting cross-gateway opportunities connecting the Association of Southeast Asian Nations markets.

 

“Hong Kong has always been the financial institution hub. Therefore, to penetrate China, I think it is best to penetrate Hong Kong first,” Malaysian delegation member Kay Moris said.

 

“We are looking at collaboration in terms of giving services to basically institutions in Hong Kong to penetrate into Southeast Asia and vice versa. So that we can also work as a collaborative partner to serve Hong Kong and China.”

 

Canada’s 20-firm delegation echoed a similar sentiment. Hong Kong Economic & Trade Office (Toronto) Head of Business & Talent Attraction/Investment Promotion Christopher Chen said: “We see Hong Kong as the trading port between Canada and China. Both countries have lots of resources that they want from each other. Invest Hong Kong plays a crucial role in introducing Canadian companies to China via the Hong Kong platform.”

 

Mr Chen also noted that prime geography, top-tier talent, and massive assets under management solidify Hong Kong’s unmatched standing across Asia.
